---
title: "Examining dictionary unknowns"
subtitle: "Measure dictionary flags and errors that remain unflagged"
description: "Learn how hunspell flags unknown workforce words and how to examine constructed spelling errors."
categories: [word processing, spell checking, workforce research]
---

A vocabulary list is almost ready for checks.
The team asks whether a spell checker can find obvious typing errors
before human checks.

Proper names and real-word typing errors complicate the task.
A dictionary finds strings absent from its entries.
It cannot establish the writer's intended meaning.

**Spell checking** here means asking hunspell for words that are absent from its
dictionary. The result is a list of unknown words, not a list of all errors.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching. The deliberate misspellings are constructed
examples from Riverton words.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- run `hunspell()` on the Riverton vocabulary.
- count word types the dictionary flags.
- build a small constructed spelling test.
- explain why known dictionary misses do not measure general error detection.
- explain why a dictionary does not flag real-word errors.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Examine the real vocabulary

The readr package imports text, and dplyr and tibble create the word list.
The purrr package applies dictionary calls to each item.
The tidytext package creates tokens, and hunspell supplies dictionary flags.
The code uses the stemming lesson's tokenization rule to build the same
lowercased 96-word vocabulary.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(tidytext)
library(hunspell)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

vocabulary <- sentences |>
  select(sentence_id, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  distinct(word) |>
  arrange(word) |>
  pull(word)

known_to_hunspell <- \(words) map_lgl(hunspell(words), \(result) length(result) == 0L)

flagged_types <- vocabulary[!known_to_hunspell(vocabulary)] |>
  sort()

flagged_table <- tibble(flagged_word_type = flagged_types)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  flagged_table,
  col.names = "Flagged word type",
  caption = "Riverton word types flagged by hunspell",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(length(vocabulary), 96L),
  identical(length(flagged_types), 2L),
  identical(flagged_types, c("october", "riverton"))
)
```

Hunspell flags 2 of the 96 source word types, `october` and `riverton`.
These are a lowercased month name and a fictional place name.
The flags indicate dictionary unknowns, not proven spelling errors.

## Build a constructed error test

The next table uses eight deliberate misspellings of real Riverton word types.
This is a constructed test, not a claim about how often people make these
errors.

```{r}
constructed_errors <- tribble(
  ~correct_word, ~misspelled_word,
  "training", "traning",
  "provided", "provied",
  "experience", "experiance",
  "required", "requiered",
  "workers", "wrokers",
  "schedules", "scheduels",
  "communication", "communciation",
  "certificate", "certficate"
)

suggestions <- hunspell_suggest(constructed_errors$misspelled_word)

constructed_results <- constructed_errors |>
  mutate(
    flagged = !known_to_hunspell(misspelled_word),
    correct_word_wrongly_flagged = !known_to_hunspell(correct_word),
    suggestion_count = map_int(suggestions, length),
    suggestions = map_chr(suggestions, \(result) paste(result, collapse = ", "))
  )

spell_summary <- tibble(
  real_errors_caught = sum(constructed_results$flagged),
  constructed_errors = nrow(constructed_results),
  correct_words_wrongly_flagged = sum(constructed_results$correct_word_wrongly_flagged),
  correct_words_checked = nrow(constructed_results),
  caught_fraction = paste0(real_errors_caught, "/", constructed_errors),
  false_flag_fraction = paste0(correct_words_wrongly_flagged, "/", correct_words_checked)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  constructed_results,
  col.names = c("Correct Riverton word", "Constructed misspelling", "Flagged", "Correct word flagged", "Suggestions returned", "Suggestions"),
  caption = "Constructed spelling errors and hunspell suggestions",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  spell_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Errors flagged",
    "Constructed errors",
    "Correct words wrongly flagged",
    "Correct words examined",
    "Flagged fraction",
    "False flag fraction"
  ),
  caption = "Counts from the constructed spelling test",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(constructed_results$flagged, rep(TRUE, 8)),
  identical(constructed_results$correct_word_wrongly_flagged, rep(FALSE, 8)),
  all(constructed_results$suggestion_count > 0L),
  identical(spell_summary$real_errors_caught, 8L),
  identical(spell_summary$correct_words_wrongly_flagged, 0L),
  identical(spell_summary$caught_fraction, "8/8"),
  identical(spell_summary$false_flag_fraction, "0/8")
)
```

Hunspell flags all 8 constructed misspellings.
Each is a non-word absent from this dictionary.
It incorrectly flags 0 of the 8 source words.
Those source words exclude the two known dictionary unknowns.
The selected examples show expected dictionary behavior, not general spelling
quality. The next example addresses an excluded error type.

## Show the real-word limit

A dictionary will not flag a typo if the typo is also a real word. `form` and
`from` are both dictionary words.

```{r}
real_word_error <- tibble(
  intended_word = "from",
  typed_word = "form",
  intended_flagged = !known_to_hunspell(intended_word),
  typed_flagged = !known_to_hunspell(typed_word)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  real_word_error,
  col.names = c("Intended word", "Typed word", "Intended word flagged", "Typed word flagged"),
  caption = "A real-word typo absent from the dictionary flags",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(real_word_error$intended_flagged, FALSE),
  identical(real_word_error$typed_flagged, FALSE),
  known_to_hunspell("form"),
  known_to_hunspell("from")
)
```

If a writer meant `from` and typed `form`, this dictionary reports no problem.
Both strings are dictionary entries. Detecting the error requires context.

## What to remember

- `hunspell()` returns dictionary unknowns.
- Unknown does not always mean misspelled.
- Individual checks of the 96 word types flag `october` and `riverton`.
- The constructed 8/8 check is a demonstration because it contains only non-word
  errors.
- Real-word errors need context as well as a dictionary.

Use hunspell to create a queue for checks. Read the flagged words in context.
A dictionary separates known and unknown strings.
People must still decide whether the sentence is correct.
